title: Mars Tracker
narrative: Where things stand on 27 October 2026. Two NASA rovers are working on the surface: Curiosity and Perseverance. Perseverance set a new distance record on 11 October (45.22 km, past the 45.16 km that NASA's Opportunity rover drove). Japan's Martian Moons eXploration probe (MMX) launched on 20 October and is on its way; arrival at Mars is August 2027 per ESA and NASASpaceFlight [JAXA's own release gives no arrival date].

Money and politics: a stopgap funding law keeps NASA at its 2026 level of $24.4 billion through 11 December 2026. The White House asked for $18.8 billion for 2027, and the House committee bill kept NASA flat at $24.4 billion. Mars Sample Return (bringing Perseverance's rock tubes to Earth) was cancelled and has no replacement plan. Two bid protests (formal challenges to a contract award) are now open at the Government Accountability Office (GAO) against NASA's Mars Telecommunications Network award to Blue Origin; the second was filed on 23 October.

Plans from companies and agencies are goals, not funded schedules, unless the entry says otherwise. They are marked [aspirational]. Facts I could not match to a second source are marked [unconfirmed]. A sol is one Martian day, about 24 hours 39 minutes.

feed.who: Scholar (Grok Bot research agent) for Tom Goldberger
feed.text: Scholar's Mars exploration course is published: how Mars has been explored, a map set, where each mission stands, and what is planned. Its facts were checked on 27 October 2026 and carry its own labels, [unconfirmed] and [aspirational], which this page keeps. This tracker starts from the course and re-checked its time-sensitive items against NASA, JAXA, GAO, ESA, UAE and Xinhua pages today. Where the course and a primary source differ, this page follows the primary source and says so (for example: the Xinhua interview with Tianwen-3's chief scientist is dated 3 September, not 4 September; and a second GAO protest exists).
feed.evidence: our own course; each fact is attributed inside it

feed.text: Posts that scientists are using instruments on Perseverance to study the dust on Mars and how it could harm future crews and equipment (the post's subject is the dust study NASA also lists on the Perseverance mission page).
feed.evidence: official NASA account; the linked JPL news article returned an access error (403) to my reader, so I could not read the article itself and give no figures from it
feed.other: NASA's Perseverance mission page lists the story under the headline "NASA's Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust".

feed.who: NASA Mars 2020 team blog, "Tinga's Tale", by Margaret Deahn (Purdue University)
feed.text: Describes a target named "Tinga" at the southern border of "Idubi", an outcrop made mostly of olivine (an igneous mineral). At Tinga the lower rock is likely a breccia (rock made of broken, angular pieces, often formed by an impact), and higher dark rocks may be part of the Idubi olivine unit or breccia that was "baked" by contact with it. The team says more study is needed. The image is from sol 2009 (14 October 2026). The post is dated 26 October on NASA's site; the author's note says it was written 19 October.
feed.evidence: official NASA blog, named author (Margaret Deahn, a Purdue University Ph.D. candidate); the geology is the team's reading, not settled

feed.who: U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO), docket B-424825.2; protester Rocket Lab USA
feed.kind: primary source (court-like docket); the protester has a business interest
feed.text: A second bid protest was filed on 23 October by Rocket Lab USA against solicitation 80GSFC26R0011, the same solicitation number as the first protest. Status: open. GAO's decision date shown is 1 February 2027. The docket does not say what the second protest argues, so I do not know how it differs from the first.
feed.evidence: GAO's own docket page; reasons not published there
feed.other: The first protest, B-424825.1 (also Rocket Lab), was filed 11 September and has a decision due 21 December 2026.

feed.text: Reports that ESA's Mars Express, at Mars since 2003, could support MMX when it arrives in 2027, with joint observations and imaging of the landing site. Says Mars Express's latest extension runs to 2029 and, quoting a former team member, is "definitely the last" (the same person notes the first "last ever extension" was around 2007). Says JAXA reported on 21 October that MMX's initial critical operations, including solar array deployment, were complete. Says MMX plans to collect about 10 g from Phobos, with return in 2031, and that ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter, not Mars Express, will be the main relay for the Rosalind Franklin rover.
feed.evidence: named reporter; the 2029 date comes from the article, not from ESA [unconfirmed against ESA]; ESA's June 2026 release says only that Mars Express was extended
feed.other: ESA's 11 June 2026 release lists Mars Express among missions given extensions, with no end date in the text I read.

feed.who: JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), launch release
feed.text: JAXA announces that MMX launched on H3 flight No. 10 at 04:41:03 Japan time on 20 October 2026 (19:41 UTC on 19 October) from the Tanegashima Space Center. The rocket flew as planned; the spacecraft separated 71 minutes 13 seconds after liftoff and was placed in its planned orbit. The release gives no Mars arrival date.
feed.other: Arrival: ESA says MMX enters Mars orbit in August 2027 and orbits Phobos from September 2027; NASASpaceFlight (Justin Davenport, 19 Oct) also says August 2027. ESA says the Phobos landing is in 2030; NASASpaceFlight says the landings come no earlier than December 2028. Those two disagree, so the landing date is [unconfirmed]. JAXA's press kit, seen only in search results, gives fiscal years only.

feed.who: NASA Curiosity team blog, sols 5036-5042, by Alex Innanen (York University)
feed.text: Says a new Mars year, number 39, began at the end of September and it is now autumn in Gale crater. The team finished a drill campaign at "Basque Lakes" (including one more gas-analysis experiment by the SAM instrument) and planned to drive back toward the "Chiu Chiu" region, where it had seen crystal forms. The first high-altitude twilight clouds of the season showed up. Earth planning date was 9 October; the image is from sol 5037 (7 October 2026).
feed.evidence: official NASA blog, named author (Alex Innanen, York University); the sol-to-date arithmetic elsewhere on this page is ours

feed.text: On Starship's tenth birthday: SpaceX's Starship has not flown to Mars; this year's Mars window (the roughly 26-month period when Earth and Mars line up for a launch) is closing with no Starship Mars launch; the next window is late 2028 to early 2029. Says Starship Flight 14 on 28 September reached orbit and that Flights 15 and 16 have no confirmed dates.
feed.evidence: named reporter summarizing company statements; no new SpaceX statement quoted for dates [aspirational]
feed.other: SpaceX's own Mars page (read 27 Oct) says Starship cargo flights to the Martian surface start "no earlier than 2028" [aspirational]. I found no Elon Musk post about a Mars launch date between 13 and 27 October; the only Mars-related post I found was a 16 October post about his Roadster car, a quip and not a program statement.

feed.who: Vandi Verma, chief engineer for robotic operations, NASA JPL (Perseverance blog)
feed.where: NASA science blog, "Tracks Along the Longest Drive on Another World"
feed.text: Verma (post dated 12 October, published 21 October) says the odometer read 45.22 km (28.10 miles) on sol 2006 and explains the driving upgrades behind it: a higher tilt limit (24 degrees), smaller required belly clearance (20 cm), new braking and wheel-slip software, and an on-board position-finding tool that works like GPS on a world without it. About 200 meters short of the record on sol 1947, the team stayed to study outcrops instead of driving on. She says the team is exploring using generative AI to help plan paths.
feed.evidence: official NASA blog, named author; the AI use is described as being explored, not in use

feed.who: NASA science editorial team, "NASA's Perseverance Sets Off-World Record for Total Distance Driven"
feed.text: NASA says Perseverance passed the record for total distance driven on another world, held by NASA's Opportunity rover: 45.22 km (28.10 miles) on sol 2006 (11 October 2026) against Opportunity's 45.16 km (28.06 miles); that day's drive was 91.31 meters. It took Perseverance about five and a half years; Opportunity took almost 15. NASA also says the mission's first extension began in October and runs to roughly the end of 2028, and that the rover is heading toward "Idubi" and then south toward a block of uplifted ancient crust called Rainbow Falls. NASA says Perseverance has collected 29 rock and regolith samples (CNN counts 33 tubes, which also includes dust and air samples).

Reports that Mars Sample Return was cancelled with no clear alternative. Quotes a July NASA statement: NASA is "exploring a range of potential return options" that could be simpler and cheaper, "including possible commercial or international contributions". Quotes NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman (30 August): "There's no question we're going to go get samples", robot or astronaut, with no time frame. Says Perseverance has filled 33 tubes (NASA's own count of rock and regolith samples is 29), and that China's Tianwen-3 aims to return its own samples in 2031.
feed.evidence: named reporter; NASA statement and Isaacman quotes as printed; Lockheed Martin's under-$3 billion return concept (by 2037) is a company claim [aspirational]

feed.who: Rocket Lab USA, first protest at GAO (docket B-424825.1)
feed.kind: primary source (docket); the protester has a business interest
feed.text: Rocket Lab filed a bid protest against NASA's award of the Mars Telecommunications Network contract. GAO's page shows status open and a decision due 21 December 2026.

feed.who: Xinhua (China's state news agency), interview with Hou Zengqian, chief scientist of Tianwen-3
feed.text: Hou says the Tianwen-3 Mars sample-return mission is at the engineering prototype stage, that its landing site is expected to be settled by the end of 2026, and that China will build a planetary protection laboratory for the returned samples. [aspirational: no funded launch date is stated in this interview.]
feed.evidence: state media account of an official; Scholar's course dated this interview 4 September, the Xinhua page is dated 3 September
feed.other: Xinhua on 24 April 2026 reported Tianwen-3 targets a launch around 2028 and a sample return around 2031, with eight candidate landing zones [aspirational].

feed.text: Reports the stopgap spending law (continuing resolution, or CR) was signed on 2 September (Public Law 119-103). It holds NASA at its 2026 level of $24.4 billion through 11 December 2026. The White House requested $18.8 billion for 2027. Midterm elections are 3 November.

feed.who: NASA, news release "NASA Selects Blue Origin as Mars Telecommunications Network Provider"
feed.text: NASA announces it selected Blue Origin to provide the Mars Telecommunications Network (MTN), a relay satellite service for future Mars missions. NASA's April slides give the program as about $700 million. Blue Origin is a company with its own interest in the result.
Curiosity reached 1 kilometer of elevation gain on its climb up Mount Sharp (26 August, per NASA's mission page and the course's source link).
feed.evidence: NASA mission page; the dedicated news link was cited in the course and I did not open it

feed.who: Daniel Estévez, amateur radio tracker (not an agency)
feed.text: Posted "Tianwen-1 safe mode telemetry", about radio signals he tracks from China's Tianwen-1 orbiter. Per Scholar's course and his blog: a gap in signal in December 2025, the signal returned, and a safe-mode event on 2 August 2026, after which telemetry looked normal. He is an independent amateur.
feed.evidence: amateur, careful and well known; I read his blog home page and his March 2026 post, not the 7 August post itself [unconfirmed by China]

board.s: Working. Drilling at Basque Lakes (42nd drill hole), then driving on. Climbing Mount Sharp; 1 km of elevation gain reached 26 Aug 2026. FY2027 request keeps it funded at $38.0M.

Working. World-record 45.22 km driven by sol 2006 (11 Oct). Exploring the Jezero rim near the Idubi outcrop. NASA counts 29 rock and regolith samples collected, none returned; first mission extension began in October, to about end of 2028. FY2027 request would cut operations from $87.5M (2024) to $38.0M.

Asleep since May 2022; it did not wake up. China has not said the mission is over. Zhang Rongqiao, the mission's chief designer, has said dust was the most likely cause (per the Planetary Society and marsprogress.com).
board.d: Not re-checked at CNSA today; secondary source 6 Oct 2026 [unconfirmed]

board.s: Operating, "nominal, Extended Mission 5" (NASA, April 2026). FY2027 request funds it at $26.0M.
Operating, "nominal" (NASA, April 2026). Not named in the FY2027 request, which AAS (the American Astronomical Society) reads as another proposal to end it.

board.m: ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, TGO (ESA/Roscosmos program, run by ESA)
board.s: Operating, and the main relay for ESA's Rosalind Franklin rover (The Register, 22 Oct). FY2027 request continues U.S. support at $2.0M (AAS). I did not open an ESA page on TGO today.

At Mars since 2003 (The Register). ESA lists it among missions extended in June 2026 (no end date in the text). The Register (22 Oct) says the latest extension runs to 2029 and calls it the last [secondary source; not confirmed on an ESA page]. The course had said funding was secure only to end of 2026, with 2029 proposed.

Operating. The UAE Space Agency announced on 17 Feb 2026 that the mission is extended, through 2028. Course: more than 10 terabytes of data returned (The National; WAM; not re-checked for the figure).

Operating. CNSA said in April 2026 it had kept surveying Mars (reported via Xinhua on marsprogress.com). Amateur tracker Daniel Estévez saw a radio gap in Dec 2025, the signal return, and a safe-mode event on 2 Aug 2026 [amateur sourced; China has said little].

Launched 20 Oct 2026 (04:41 Japan time). Reached Mars orbit: August 2027 per ESA and NASASpaceFlight; JAXA's launch release gives no date. Phobos landing: 2030 per ESA, no earlier than December 2028 per NASASpaceFlight [unconfirmed]. Samples back on Earth in 2031 (ESA; The Register).

board.m: ESCAPADE, two orbiters (NASA and UC Berkeley)
board.s: Launched 13 Nov 2025 on Blue Origin's New Glenn. The Mars departure burn is in November 2026 and arrival is September 2027 per the Berkeley mission-design page. NASA's own page says only "fall of 2026" for the Earth flyby. FY2027 request: $4.5M.

Ended. Last heard 6 Dec 2025; NASA declared the mission ended 3 June 2026. An anomaly review board found it unrecoverable. The root cause is still being investigated, with a final report expected later this year (per Scholar's course; not re-read today).
Ended 21 Dec 2022 after recording 1,319 marsquakes (per Scholar's course).
Ended 25 Jan 2024 after 72 flights (per Scholar's course).
Silent; end of mission per the course [unconfirmed here].

perseverance.area: Southern border of "Idubi", an olivine-rich outcrop on the rim of Jezero crater; the rover's recent target there is called "Tinga".
perseverance.est_note: our own arithmetic: sol 2009 = 14 Oct, and one sol is about 1.0275 Earth days. NASA has not posted a newer sol in the sources I opened.
perseverance.note: "Last waypoint in NASA's file" is the newest point in NASA's public traverse file (a list of the rover's stopping points). That file does not update every day. The record figure of 45.22 km was for sol 2006 (11 Oct); the file's sol 2009 figure is 45,223.6 meters, which rounds to the same 45.22 km. If NASA's blog is newer, the daily check uses the blog's numbers.

curiosity.t: Latest NASA blog: sols 5036 to 5042, posted 19 October 2026 by Alex Innanen. Drill campaign at "Basque Lakes"; it is autumn in Gale crater; a new Mars year (number 39) began at the end of September.

Sol 5037 was 7 October 2026 per the blog's own dates, so 27 October is about sol 5056 (our own arithmetic). NASA's page in the sources I opened gives no odometer for 27 October, so none is shown here.
Climbing Mount Sharp, the mound in Gale crater: 1 kilometer of elevation gain reached on 26 August 2026, per NASA's mission page, which also counts 42 drill holes.

Distance: NASA's 12 October record release says Curiosity has driven more than 38.07 km (23.65 miles). Money: the FY2027 request puts Curiosity (the Mars Science Laboratory line) at $38.0M, from $40.0M in the 2024 plan (AAS summary of NASA's request); Congress has not set the final 2027 number.

money.t: Mars Sample Return (MSR): no approved program. NASA's 2026 request said it "plans to terminate" MSR. For 2027, AAS says the request "reiterates the cancellation", while CNN's Ashley Strickland says the request does not mention the program at all; the two read the document differently. NASA's July 2026 statement: it is "exploring a range of potential return options" that are simpler and cheaper, "including possible commercial or international contributions". The 2026 spending law gave $110 million for Mars Future Missions (NASA slides); the Planetary Society says it was meant to buy down technical risk for a restructured sample return. The Planetary Society, an advocacy group for space exploration, says the House committee bill for 2027 is "silent" on MSR.

2027 request versus Congress. White House request (3 April 2026): NASA $18.829 billion, 23% below the $24.438 billion enacted for 2026; Planetary Science $1.876 billion (down 26%); Mars Exploration $248.3 million; Perseverance operations $38.0 million, down from $87.5 million in the 2024 plan (AAS says NASA is "reassessing objectives for the mission"); Mars Future Missions $110 million (American Astronomical Society, AAS, summary of NASA's request). House Appropriations Committee bill (13 May): NASA flat at $24.4 billion, Planetary Science $2.5 billion, Mars Exploration $300 million (Planetary Society tables; the full House has not passed it as far as I read). Senate: SpacePolicyOnline reported on 1 September that no Senate appropriations bill had been reported. Stopgap law P.L. 119-103 (signed 2 September) keeps NASA at the 2026 level through 11 December 2026.

Missions the request does not mention (AAS reads these as proposed endings, carried over from the 2026 request): Mars Odyssey, the U.S. part of Mars Express, and the U.S. contribution to ESA's Rosalind Franklin rover. The House committee report protects some other science missions; I did not confirm it names these three.

Blue Origin's Mars Telecommunications Network (MTN, a relay network for Mars): NASA selected Blue Origin on 1 September 2026 (NASA release). NASA's April slides give about $700 million total, a fixed-price contract.

The protests against the MTN award, both by Rocket Lab USA at the GAO: B-424825.1 filed 11 September, decision due 21 December 2026; B-424825.2 filed 23 October, decision date shown 1 February 2027. Both open. Rocket Lab is a competitor with its own interest. GAO's pages do not state the arguments.

Low-cost Mars mission solicitation: the 2027 request (AAS summary of NASA's document) says a low-cost mission solicitation "will be released in October 2026", targeting a 2030 launch at a $220 million lifecycle cost, not counting the rocket. As of 27 October I did not find it released on NASA's Mars pages: not yet seen [unconfirmed]. [aspirational until funded.] NASA's April slides name launch windows FY29, FY31 and FY33 as considerations.
Politics to watch: midterm elections 3 November 2026; the stopgap ends 11 December. Congress, not the White House request, sets the final amounts.

plans.t: Says Starship cargo flights to the Martian surface start no earlier than 2028 and prices cargo at $100 million per metric ton. In February 2026 Elon Musk said the company would for now give priority to a city on the Moon (The Guardian, as cited in the course; I did not open it). Flight 14 reached orbit on 28 September (Space.com).
plans.label: aspirational

plans.t: NASA's April slides say a nuclear-electric spacecraft, SR-1 Freedom, targets Mars in 2028 and would release "SkyFall" helicopters. The House committee bill supports it, and the Planetary Society repeats NASA's plan to fly it "before the end of 2028". Funding is not final.
plans.label: aspirational

plans.t: Launch about 2028, samples back about 2031. Eight candidate landing zones; final site expected by end of 2026; at the engineering prototype stage (Xinhua, April and September 2026). Two launches, one lander with a drill and a helicopter (CNN, citing the mission team's 2025 paper).
plans.label: aspirational

plans.who: ESA with NASA: Rosalind Franklin rover (ExoMars)
plans.t: NASA began implementation of its part in April 2026. NASA's April slides say "scheduled to launch in 2028"; the course says no earlier than late 2028, with a late-2030 landing reported [unconfirmed]. The 2027 U.S. budget request does not mention the U.S. contribution.
plans.label: aspirational

plans.t: A lander-and-orbiter follow-up to India's first Mars mission. The only on-record statement I opened: Nilesh Desai, a director at ISRO, told ANI on 8 October 2025 that work has begun and that it "will be completed by 2028-2030", and that the trip takes 10 months. No official launch date or approved budget found [unconfirmed].
plans.label: aspirational

plans.t: No agency has an approved, funded, dated crewed mission to Mars as of 27 October 2026 that I could find. NASA calls Mars a "horizon goal" after the Moon (course, citing NASA release 26-025, which I did not open). Treat any crewed-Mars date, from SpaceX or anyone, as a goal.
plans.label: aspirational

plans.who: NASA: Mars Future Missions and the low-cost mission
plans.t: A $110 million technology and low-cost-mission line, a planned solicitation aimed at a 2030 launch, and a payload program. See Money and politics.
plans.label: aspirational

upcoming: U.S. midterm elections; Congress makes little progress before this (SpacePolicyOnline).
ESCAPADE leaves Earth's neighborhood for Mars (burn in November per Berkeley's mission-design page; NASA says only "fall 2026"). Exact date not published [unconfirmed].
Starship Flights 15 and 16: slipped to mid or late November per Space.com; no confirmed dates.
The stopgap spending law (P.L. 119-103) runs out.
GAO decision due on the first MTN protest (B-424825.1).
Tianwen-3 landing site expected to be chosen (Xinhua).
Date shown on GAO's page for the second MTN protest (B-424825.2).
MMX enters Mars orbit (ESA, NASASpaceFlight; JAXA gives fiscal year 2027 only). Orbit around Phobos from September 2027 per ESA.
ESCAPADE arrives at Mars (Berkeley mission-design page).

Rosalind Franklin launch (NASA's April slides say 2028; the course says no earlier than late 2028); Tianwen-3 launch about 2028; SR-1 Freedom before end of 2028; SpaceX Starship Mars cargo "no earlier than 2028"; Hope extended through 2028. Next Mars launch window: late 2028 to early 2029.
Mars Express mission reported to run to 2029 (The Register) [unconfirmed against ESA].
MMX Phobos landing per ESA (NASASpaceFlight says December 2028 at the earliest) [unconfirmed]. Mangalyaan-2 window "2028-2030" per ISRO's Desai [unconfirmed]. NASA low-cost mission launch target.
Samples from Phobos return to Earth (MMX, ESA); Tianwen-3 sample return (Xinhua).
glossary: one Martian day, about 24 hours 39 minutes. Rovers count their days in sols from landing.
the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, an instrument that measured Mars's heights by laser; used for the course's maps.
in-situ resource use: making water, air or fuel from what is already on Mars instead of bringing it.
a company challenges a federal contract award at the Government Accountability Office, which must decide within about 100 days.
continuing resolution: a stopgap law that keeps agencies funded at last year's level while Congress finishes the new budget.
the roughly 26-month period when Earth and Mars line up well for a launch.
